title: Bodily Discharges and the Holy Tabernacle
summary: The LORD gives laws about uncleanness caused by discharges from the genitals of men and women: a man's abnormal discharge, an emission of semen, sexual intercourse, a woman's monthly period, and prolonged bleeding outside it. Each case explains how uncleanness spreads to beds, seats, and people, and how long it lasts. The chapter ends by stating its purpose: to keep Israel from defiling the tabernacle that stands among them.
story: This is the last of the laws on clean and unclean that began in Leviticus 11. The sequence has moved from food, to childbirth, to skin disease and mildew, and now to the most private matters of the body. Verse 31 explains why all of it matters: God's tabernacle is “among them”, in the middle of the camp, so the ordinary facts of bodily life have to be managed in relation to his presence. The next chapter, the Day of Atonement, will deal with every uncleanness the people have brought on the sanctuary over a year, including ones the laws of chapters 11 to 15 could not catch. Chapter 15 therefore finishes the diagnosis before chapter 16 provides the great annual remedy.
historical:
As with the surrounding chapters, the book sets this law at Sinai during the wilderness period, and its date of composition is debated along the usual lines (Mosaic tradition, or priestly material shaped over time and edited in or after the exile, or older practice written down later). Rules about bodily fluids and access to sacred places were common across the ancient world. Texts from Egypt, Mesopotamia, and the Hittite kingdom include requirements for priests and worshipers to be pure before entering a temple, and some peoples restricted menstruating women from sacred areas. Israel's law shares that general concern but places it in a very different frame.

The practical life behind the chapter was that of a village household. Beds were often mats or mattresses on the floor, seats were simple, and clay pots were porous, which is why a clay pot touched by a man with a discharge had to be broken while a wooden utensil could simply be rinsed (verse 12). Water for bathing was drawn from springs, cisterns, or streams. Later Judaism developed immersion pools (the mikveh) for this kind of washing, and many have been excavated from the Second Temple period, but that institution belongs to a later time than the text.
cultural:
Two ideas a modern reader has to set aside. First, being unclean was not being sinful. Nothing in the chapter blames anyone. A husband and wife who have intercourse (verse 18) are unclean until evening, yet marriage and children are blessings throughout the Old Testament. Uncleanness was a temporary status that barred a person from the sanctuary and holy food, and it ended with washing, waiting, and, for longer conditions, an offering. Second, the laws apply to men and women alike. The chapter begins with men, and men who touch unclean things are as affected as women.

Many scholars explain the logic this way: the fluids named here are tied to life and its loss. Blood carries life (Leviticus 17:11) and semen carries the potential for life, so their loss marked a brush with mortality, and the God of life was kept apart from the signs of death. Others add that separating sexual activity from worship set Israel apart from religions in which sexual rites were part of temple practice, though how widespread such rites actually were in Canaan is debated. Whatever the full explanation, the effect was that every household in Israel lived with a constant, daily awareness that the holy God was near.
literary: The chapter is built symmetrically, a pattern many commentators have noted. It moves from a man's abnormal, long-term discharge (verses 2 to 15), to a man's normal emission (16 and 17), to the act that involves both a man and a woman (18), then to a woman's normal period (19 to 24) and her abnormal, long-term bleeding (25 to 30). The long-term cases at each end require seven days of waiting and an offering on the eighth day; the ordinary cases need no offering, only washing and waiting, until evening for a man's emission and for intercourse, and seven days for a woman's period. Intercourse stands at the center, where man and woman are treated together. Phrases repeat with the steadiness of a legal code, above all “wash his clothes and bathe with water, and he will be unclean until evening”. Verses 31 to 33 close with the purpose and a summary.

outline.t: A man's abnormal discharge and how uncleanness spreads
Cleansing and offering after the discharge ends
Emission of semen and sexual intercourse
The purpose: protecting the tabernacle among the people

doctrines.note: Verse 31 is the key: God dwells among Israel, and his holiness reaches into the most ordinary parts of life. Holiness is not confined to the sanctuary; it shapes the bedroom, the kitchen, and the saddle.

The chapter treats the body frankly and without shame. Sexuality and menstruation are not sinful, but they belong to mortal human life, and the law marks the difference between that life and the undying life of God.

For long-term conditions, the person brings a purification offering and a burnt offering, and the priest makes atonement. Atonement here restores access to God after impurity, not only forgiveness after wrongdoing.

words.note: Zov, a flow or discharge. The word is used mostly in this chapter and a few related laws. It covers an abnormal flow from the body, for a man probably some kind of genital infection and for a woman bleeding beyond her normal period. The BSB renders it discharge.

Niddah, menstrual impurity or separation. The word can describe the monthly period itself and the state of separation it brought. Later prophets used it as a metaphor for moral defilement (for example, Ezekiel 36:17), but in this chapter it describes a natural condition without moral blame.

Tum'ah, uncleanness, the state that results from these conditions. Verse 31 uses the same root for the danger that uncleanness poses to the tabernacle. It spreads by contact and is removed by time, washing, and in some cases sacrifice.

Erev, evening. Most of the uncleanness in this chapter lasts until evening, when a new day began in Israelite reckoning. The word appears 15 times, a reminder that many forms of impurity were brief, ordinary, and easily cleared.

christ: The Gospels tell of a woman who had suffered from bleeding for twelve years (Mark 5:25-34; Matthew 9:20-22; Luke 8:43-48). Under verses 25 to 27 she would have been unclean for all those years, and anyone she touched would have become unclean. She reaches through a crowd and touches Jesus's garment, and instead of her uncleanness passing to him, his healing passes to her. Jesus stops, seeks her out, and calls her daughter, publicly restoring the person the law had kept at the edges. This does not abolish the chapter in the story; it shows the reality the chapter was pointing toward, a holiness that is stronger than impurity and can make the unclean clean. The New Testament also teaches that in Christ believers are made clean and have access to God's presence (Hebrews 10:19-22), which Christians have generally understood to mean that the purity laws of Leviticus no longer govern access to worship, though they still reveal God's holiness.

hard.q: Does this chapter treat women's bodies as shameful or dirty?
hard.a:
Many modern readers feel that it does, and the concern deserves a straight answer. The chapter's structure does not single out women: it begins with men, applies the same kind of rules to both sexes, and places the case of man and woman together at its center. Uncleanness in Leviticus was not a moral judgment, and it was shared by anyone who touched a corpse, had a skin disease, or had marital relations. A woman's period made her unclean for seven days, which in practice meant regular periods when she could not go to the sanctuary, but it was a status, not a verdict on her.

It is also true that the law's effects fell unevenly. A woman's monthly cycle meant more frequent impurity than most men experienced, and later traditions sometimes expanded these rules in ways that did marginalize women. Readers disagree about how much of that pressure lies in the text and how much in its later use. What the text itself states is its reason (verse 31), which is about the presence of God, not the worth of women, and the Gospels show Jesus welcoming a woman whose bleeding had made her an outsider.

questions: Uncleanness in this chapter was part of ordinary life, not a sin. How might that distinction help someone who feels ashamed of their body or its weaknesses?
Verse 31 says God's dwelling was among them. How might living with that kind of awareness shape the ordinary, private parts of your life?
The woman who touched Jesus's garment had been on the edges for twelve years. Who in your community lives with a condition that quietly keeps them at a distance?
